name: Office English Starter
lede: Your first four weeks of useful work English, made simple. Learn the words you’ll actually use in meetings, messages, and deadlines — and start using them on Monday.
outcome: The everyday words for meetings, messages, and deadlines — enough to get through your first month at work.
outcomes: Join a meeting, ask a simple question, and understand what happens next.
Write a short update or email that people can read and reply to.
Talk about dates and deadlines without checking your notes twice.

aside.title: A gentle start, not a grammar lesson.
aside.body: These are the words you’ll hear on your first day and use every week after. Learn a few, say them out loud, and don’t worry about getting them perfect.

words.definition: A short list of topics to talk about in a meeting.
words.example: I added your question to the agenda for Monday.

words.definition: To check back with someone after a meeting or message.
words.example: I’ll follow up with the client tomorrow morning.

words.definition: The latest time or day when work must be finished.
words.example: The deadline for the report is Friday at noon.

words.definition: A short warning about something that is going to happen.
words.example: Thanks for the heads-up about the early meeting.

words.definition: A short daily meeting where everyone shares a quick update.
words.example: We have a standup every morning at nine.

words.definition: A plan that shows when meetings and tasks will happen.
words.example: My schedule is quite full on Wednesday afternoon.

words.definition: To move a meeting or task to a different time.
words.example: Can we reschedule the call to Thursday afternoon?

words.definition: A file you add to an email for someone to open.
words.example: Please check the attachment for the full report.

words.definition: To add someone to an email so they can see it.
words.example: Please cc me on the reply to the client.

words.definition: To answer everyone who received the same email.
words.example: Don’t reply all unless everyone really needs to know.

words.definition: A message that says you are away and cannot reply.
words.example: I’ll be out of office until Monday morning.

words.definition: To write down the important points during a meeting.
words.example: Can you take notes while I lead the call?

words.definition: The written record of what was said in a meeting.
words.example: I’ll send the minutes after the meeting ends.

words.definition: New information about how a task or project is going.
words.example: Can you give me a quick update on the project?

words.definition: A piece of work you need to finish.
words.example: I have three tasks to finish before lunch today.

words.definition: Someone who works with you on the same team.
words.example: My teammate will cover the meeting for me.

words.definition: The person in charge of your team and your work.
words.example: My manager approved my leave request this morning.

words.definition: A customer or company that pays for your work.
words.example: The client wants a simpler version of the design.

words.definition: The day by which a piece of work must be done.
words.example: The due date for the draft is next Tuesday.

words.definition: To ask someone how their work is going.
words.example: I’ll check in with you after lunch today.

words.definition: To give official approval to a plan or document.
words.example: My manager needs to sign off on the budget.

words.definition: To give finished work to the person who asked for it.
words.example: Please hand in your timesheet by Friday afternoon.

words.definition: To say that something is definitely happening or correct.
words.example: Please confirm the meeting time by email today.

words.definition: Free to meet or talk at a certain time.
words.example: Are you available for a quick call at three?
